summary: The paper introduces a quantum truncated mean estimator (QTME) for heavy‑tailed distributions achieving estimation error O(n^{-2v/(1+v)}) versus the classical O(n^{-v/(1+v)}). Using this primitive, the authors propose Heavy‑QUCB and Heavy‑QLinUCB algorithms with theoretical regret bounds O(KT^{(1−v)/(1+v)} log T) for MAB and O(d²T^{(1−v)/(1+v)}) (up to logs) for SLB, improving the classical heavy‑tailed regret Θ(T^{1/(1+v)}). All empirical results are classical simulations with T=10^6 rounds and K=5 arms.

experiments.description: Simulation study of the proposed quantum mean estimator (QTME/QBME) for heavy-tailed one-dimensional reward distributions as a subroutine for quantum bandits.

algorithm.variant: Quantum Truncated Mean Estimator (QTME) built on Quantum Basic Mean Estimator (QBME) and Quantum Monte Carlo Mean Estimator

hyperparameters.B: truncation bound chosen as (sqrt(u n / log(1/delta)))^(2/(1+v))

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Quantum reward oracle O_Y encodes a random variable Y by preparing amplitudes proportional to sqrt(Pr[Y=y]) over the finite sample space; QTME estimates the mean by truncating to [0,B] and applying quantum mean estimation on disjoint intervals.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate E[X] for a heavy-tailed random variable X with finite (1+v)-th raw moment.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Truncation to [0,B] and decomposition into positive/negative parts; no penalty formulation.

problem_instance.description: One-dimensional heavy-tailed random variable mean estimation used as a primitive for later bandit algorithms.

dataset_specification.description: General heavy-tailed distributions with finite (1+v)-th raw moment; no specific dataset.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Truncation of the random variable into intervals [a_{l-1}, a_l] and separate estimation of positive and negative parts.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Theoretical error bound; no separate empirical protocol specified for this subroutine beyond use in later simulations.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical simulation of the measurement output distribution of quantum amplitude estimation is mentioned for the numerical experiments.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Combine estimates of truncated segments and positive/negative parts to form the mean estimate.

results.unit: oracle queries up to logarithmic factors

speedup_claims.factor: quadratic improvement in estimation error exponent
speedup_claims.conditions: for random variables with finite (1+v)-th raw moment and quantum oracle access
speedup_claims.caveats: Claim is asymptotic and up to logarithmic factors; no physical hardware experiment is reported.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(n) oracle queries for QTME/QBME up to logarithmic factors; mean estimation error ~ O(n^{-2v/(1+v)})
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(n) samples with mean estimation error ~ O(n^{-v/(1+v)}) for heavy-tailed distributions

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require fault‑tolerant amplitude estimation circuits implementing the QTME estimator with O(n) oracle queries.
limiting_factors: Requires coherent quantum reward oracle state preparation
Amplitude estimation circuits require deep fault‑tolerant circuits
No implementation on actual quantum hardware
Quantum advantage only expressed in oracle query complexity

notes: No actual qubit count or hardware platform is reported for the mean-estimation subroutine; it is presented as an oracle/query-complexity algorithm and simulated classically in the experiments. Hardware type inferred as simulator_other because the paper states the quantum mean estimator is simulated classically via the measurement output distribution of amplitude estimation.
The paper proves a quadratic improvement in estimation error O(n^{-2v/(1+v)}) vs classical O(n^{-v/(1+v)}), but experiments only simulate the estimator classically.

experiments.description: Numerical comparison of Heavy-QUCB versus classical robust UCB on synthetic heavy-tailed multi-armed bandit instances S1, S2, and S3.

hyperparameters.C: constant in algorithm and confidence radius

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Quantum reward oracle for each arm; no explicit qubit encoding of a combinatorial objective is given.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Maximize cumulative reward / minimize regret in heavy-tailed MAB.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: UCB selection with QTME-based confidence intervals; no penalty terms.

problem_instance.description: Synthetic 5-armed bandit with Pareto-distributed rewards and three mean-gap configurations.

dataset_specification.description: Instances S1, S2, S3; means in [0.1,1]; S1 means {0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9}; S2 quadratic convex means; S3 concave means.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Rewards sampled from Pareto distributions with shape parameter alpha=1.05+v and scale chosen to match target means; u set from the maximum (1+v)-moment bound across arms.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: 100 independent repetitions; average regret and standard deviation reported; comparison against robust UCB.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Synthetic reward generation from Pareto distributions; experiments executed on a classical computer (AMD Ryzen 7 7300X CPU with 16GB memory).
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Average regret and standard deviation over 100 runs.

results.unit: plus v for Pareto shape parameter alpha=1.05+v

speedup_claims.factor: improvement by a factor of O(T^(v/(1+v)))
speedup_claims.conditions: heavy-tailed MAB with finite (1+v)-th raw moment; quantum reward oracle; asymptotic regret bound
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports a theoretical regret improvement; the numerical section shows lower average regret but does not provide exact numeric regret values in text.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(u^{1/(1+v)} K T^{(1-v)/(1+v)} log T) regret
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(T^{1/(1+v)}) regret for heavy-tailed MAB (up to log factors)

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Requires scalable implementation of QTME within bandit rounds with repeated amplitude estimation calls.
limiting_factors: No circuit-level resource estimates (qubits, depth, gates)
Quantum reward oracle assumed but not implemented
Speedup derived from oracle query complexity rather than runtime

notes: The experiment is numerical/simulated; no physical QPU or qubit count is reported. The paper explicitly states the quantum mean estimator is simulated classically via the amplitude-estimation output distribution.
Authors claim polynomial regret improvement: quantum regret O(T^{(1−v)/(1+v)}) vs classical O(T^{1/(1+v)}).
Empirical results compare simulated quantum algorithm to classical robust UCB but do not run on quantum hardware.

experiments.description: Numerical comparison of Heavy-QLinUCB versus classical LinUCB on synthetic heavy-tailed stochastic linear bandit instances.

algorithm.variant: Heavy-QLinUCB (quantum linear UCB for heavy-tailed SLB)

hyperparameters.delta: varied; figure shows different delta values
hyperparameters.C: constant in algorithm and confidence radius

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Quantum reward oracle for each action; weighted least squares used to estimate the linear parameter from QTME outputs.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Maximize cumulative reward / minimize regret in heavy-tailed stochastic linear bandit.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Confidence sets Cs and optimistic action selection; no penalty terms.

problem_instance.description: Synthetic 2D linear bandit with 50 actions on the positive unit circle and three parameter vectors.

dataset_specification.description: Three instances: theta*_1=(cos(0.35pi), sin(0.35pi)), theta*_2=(cos(pi/6), sin(pi/6)), theta*_3=(cos(5pi/6), sin(5pi/6)); action set consists of 50 actions equally spaced on the positive part of the unit circle.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: No external dataset; synthetic action set and parameter vectors. QTME outputs are used as noisy reward estimates in weighted least squares.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: 100 independent repetitions; average regret and standard deviation reported; comparison against LinUCB; different delta values shown in Figure 3.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Synthetic linear bandit environment with 50 actions on the positive unit circle; enumeration used to solve the optimistic action selection over A × C_{s−1}.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Average regret and standard deviation over 100 runs.

speedup_claims.factor: improvement by a factor of O(T^(v/(1+v)))
speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical heavy-tailed linear bandits / LinUCB baseline in experiment
speedup_claims.conditions: heavy-tailed SLB with finite (1+v)-th raw moment; quantum reward oracle; asymptotic regret bound
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports a theoretical regret improvement and a qualitative simulation comparison; exact numeric regret values are not stated in the text.

complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(d T^{1/(1+v)}) regret for heavy-tailed SLB (up to log factors)

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Fault‑tolerant amplitude estimation subroutines embedded inside stochastic linear bandit learning loop.
limiting_factors: Algorithm evaluated only via classical simulation
Quantum oracle access assumption unrealistic for real bandit environments
Enumeration solver used for optimistic action selection in simulation

notes: The paper reports only simulation results and does not specify a quantum device or qubit count. The quantum mean estimator is simulated classically from the amplitude-estimation output distribution.
Paper claims regret improvement over classical heavy‑tailed SLB from Θ(T^{1/(1+v)}) to O(T^{(1−v)/(1+v)}).
Experimental comparison is against classical LinUCB using classical simulation.
